name: Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth
description: The humanist programme of letters, virtue, and the well-governed state: the training of princes, magistrates, and scholars, and the imagining of just societies from Utopia to the governed commonwealth of Elyot's Governour.

name: Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
description: The Reformation insistence on scripture alone, justification by faith, and the vernacular Word: Bible translation, the liturgy, and the conflict of the old church and the new over the means of salvation.

name: Courtly service and courtly danger
description: The peril and the art of serving a prince: Wyatt's coded lyrics of surveillance and disfavour, the fall of Wolsey and More, and the complaint of the courtier caught between duty, ambition, and destruction.

name: Tyranny and the abuse of power
description: The Renaissance analysis of the tyrant, from More's critique of enclosure and the politics of Utopia through Skelton's attacks on Wolsey to the Marian examinations; the claim of conscience against the commands of power.

name: The English vernacular and national letters
description: The deliberate cultivation of English (and Scots) as languages of scripture, learning, and literature: translation, the reformed grammar, the defence of the mother tongue, and the rise of a national literary canon.

name: Love, constancy, and betrayal
description: The courtly and Petrarchan thematics of the early Tudor lyric: the faithless mistress, the forsaken lover, the vow and its breaking, and the ideal of constancy tested by time and fortune.

name: Conscience and moral self-examination
description: The scrutiny of the self before God: the examination of conscience in More's prison writings and Askew's examinations, the confessional lyric, and the Tudor obsession with sincerity and the inward witness.

name: Religious persecution and martyrdom
description: The experience and literature of persecution in the Reformation: the burnings of Fisher, More, Askew, Cranmer, Latimer, and Tyndale, the examinations of the accused, and the martyrological tradition that memorialized them.

name: The education of princes and magistrates
description: The mirror-for-princes tradition: the fashioning of the ruler's wisdom, justice, and virtue in Utopia, the Governour, the interludes, and the chronicles that taught statecraft through example.
